m1.title: Identify the tools
m1.desc: The electrician's hand tools, their English names and what they're for.
m1.s1: Welcome to the shop. Let's get to know your tools. On site they're called by their English names, so learn them that way. Tap the one I ask for.
m1.w_dikes: Those are [[dikes]]: they only cut, no gripping nose.
m1.s2: Tap the [[lineman_pliers]]: thick flat nose, they cut and twist.
m1.w_needle2: Those are [[needle_nose]]. Dikes have a short angled head for cutting.
m1.s3ok: Good. Dikes cut wire and zip ties flush.
m1.s4: Tap the [[wire_strippers]]: they have numbered holes.
m1.s5: Tap the [[cable_ripper]]: the small orange one.
m1.s5ok: It slits NM-B jacket without cutting the wires inside.
m1.w_meter: That's the [[multimeter]]. The tick tester is the yellow pen.
m1.w_ncvt: That's the tick tester. The multimeter has a display and a dial.
m1.s8: Tap the [[fish_tape]]. Look for it hanging on the pegboard.
m1.s8ok: That's it. There's a coiled steel tape inside.
m1.s9: What do you use to remove the [[jacket]] of an [[nm_b]] cable without damaging the conductors?
m1.s9aFb: Dikes cut everything, including the conductor insulation.
m1.s9bFb: Exactly. It runs down the middle of the jacket without touching the conductors.
m1.s9cFb: Pulling tears or stretches the cable. Use the ripper.
m1.s10aFb: Measuring is the tape measure's job.
m1.s10b: To pass and pull wire through conduit or closed walls.
m1.s10c: To tie cables in the panel.
m1.s10cFb: You tie with zip ties. The fish tape is for pulling wire.

m2.title: AWG sizes and cable types
m2.desc: Read the gauge from the jacket color, understand the cable printing, and when to use NM-B or THHN.
m2.s1: Wire size is measured in [[awg]]. Careful, it's backwards: the BIGGER the number, the THINNER the wire. 14 is thinner than 12, and 12 thinner than 10.
m2.s2: Which of these wires is the thickest?
m2.s2aFb: No: 14 is the thinnest of the three.
m2.s2bFb: Close: 12 is thicker than 14, but there's a thicker one.
m2.s2cFb: Correct. Smaller number = thicker wire = carries more amps.
m2.s3: Houses use [[nm_b]] (people call it [[romex]]). The [[jacket]] color tells the gauge: **white = 14**, **yellow = 12**, **orange = 10**, black = 8 or 6.
m2.s4: Put each [[coil]] on its gauge sign. Go by the jacket color.
m2.s5: Grab me a roll of twelve-two. Quick.
m2.s5ok: That one. “12/2” = 12 gauge, 2 insulated conductors, plus ground.
m2.s6: Everything you need to know is printed on the jacket. Tap each point.
m2.pSizeInfo: 12 gauge, 2 insulated [[conductor]]s (black and white), and W/G = With Ground: it has a [[bare_copper]] ground.
m2.pTypeInfo: Cable type: [[nm_b]], for dry indoor use in wood-framed houses.
m2.pVoltInfo: Insulation is rated up to 600 volts. Homes use 120V and 240V.
m2.s7: This is [[thhn]]: each conductor is separate, with its own colored insulation. There's no jacket, so it's protected inside [[conduit]] like [[emt]]. Standard in commercial work.
m2.s8: You're wiring the bedrooms of a new wood-framed house. Which cable?
m2.s8aFb: Correct. Houses: NM-B stapled to the studs.
m2.s8bFb: THHN without conduit is unprotected. Never run it loose in a wall.
m2.s8cFb: Never. A cord is not permanent wiring.
m2.s9: In a commercial store everything runs in [[emt]]. What do you pull through the pipe?
m2.s9aFb: Commercial rule of thumb: THHN inside EMT. NM-B is for dwellings.
m2.s9bFb: That's it. Colored THHN conductors pulled inside the EMT.

m3.title: Color code
m3.desc: US hot, neutral and ground colors, re-identified wires and 208/120 vs 480/277 colors.
m3.s1: US colors: [[hot]] = black or red (or any color other than white, gray or green). [[neutral]] = white or gray, ALWAYS. [[ground]] = green or [[bare_copper]].
m3.s2: Put each [[thhn]] spool on its job: hot, neutral or ground.
m3.wWhiteHot: White is neutral. Only used as hot if re-identified with tape.
m3.wGreenHot: Green is ONLY ground. Never hot.
m3.wBareN: Bare copper is ground, not neutral.
m3.wWhiteG: White is neutral. Ground is green or bare.
m3.s2ok: Nice! Black and red = hot, white = neutral, green and bare = ground.
m3.s3: You open a switch box and see a white wire with black tape on the end. What is it?
m3.s3a: A normal neutral; the tape doesn't matter.
m3.s3aFb: The tape matters: it's warning you that white carries voltage.
m3.s3b: A white [[re_identify|re-identified]] as hot, e.g. in a [[switch_loop]].
m3.s3bFb: Correct. Treat it as hot. And as always: test before touching.
m3.s3cFb: Ground is green or bare. White with black tape = hot.
m3.s4: Commercial buildings use [[three_phase]]. **208Y/120V**: black, red, blue (white neutral). **480Y/277V**: brown, orange, yellow — remember [[boy]] — with a gray neutral.
m3.s5: Which system does each spool belong to? Drag it to the 208Y/120V or the 480Y/277V sign.
m3.wBlue: Blue is the third phase of 208/120 (black, red, blue).
m3.wGray: In 208/120 the neutral is white. Gray is used for the 480/277 neutral.
m3.s5ok: Great: 208 = black-red-blue; 480 = brown-orange-yellow with gray neutral.
m3.s6: You open a panel in a warehouse and see brown, orange and yellow wires. What voltage do you expect?
m3.s6aFb: No. Brown-orange-yellow signals 480V. Much more dangerous.
m3.s6bFb: Correct. Colors are a guide, not a guarantee: always measure.
m3.s6cFb: No. Those are 480V colors. Assuming low voltage kills people.

m4.title: Stripping wire
m4.desc: Pick the right hole, strip to length, spot a nicked conductor and test continuity.
m4.s1: Let's [[strip]] wire. The normal length for a device or a [[wire_nut]] is about 3/4 inch. Too short = poor contact and heat. Too long = exposed copper, a short waiting to happen.
m4.s2: You have a 12 AWG [[solid]] wire. Which hole of the [[wire_strippers]] do you use?
m4.s2aFb: Yes: right gauge and type. It cuts the insulation without touching the copper.
m4.s2b: The 14 hole: it grips tighter and strips better.
m4.s2bFb: Too small: you'll [[nick]] the copper and weaken the wire.
m4.s2cFb: Too big: it won't cut the insulation cleanly and you'll tear it.
m4.s3: Hold to strip and release at **3/4 inch**. Watch the yellow ruler next to the wire.
m4.low: Too little copper: it won't seat in the terminal and it'll heat up. Try again.
m4.high: Too much bare copper: it can touch something and short. Cut it and strip again.
m4.s4: Now a 14 AWG for a breaker. Check the breaker's [[strip_gauge]]: it calls for **1/2 inch**. Strip to that.
m4.low2: Too short for the breaker. Again.
m4.high2: Too long: copper would stick out of the breaker. Again.
m4.s4ok: Good. Every terminal has its own length: always check it.
m4.s5: A coworker stripped these two. Mark the problem and press **Report**.
m4.pNickInfo: It has a [[nick]]: the copper is bitten. It will break or heat there. Cut it off and re-strip.
m4.s5ok: Good eye. A nicked conductor gets cut off and re-stripped.
m4.s6: Before installing a wire, check it isn't broken inside. Set the [[multimeter]] to [[continuity]] (•))) ) and touch one lead to each end of the SAME wire. If it beeps, it's good.
m4.wMode: To check the wire is unbroken use continuity mode (•))) ). And remember: power off.
m4.wPoints: Both leads must be on the two ends of the SAME wire (A and B).
m4.s6ok: Beep! 0.3 Ω: the wire is continuous.
m4.s7: Excellent. Right hole, right length, no nicks, and when in doubt, test continuity. That's clean work.

m5.title: Wire to breaker
m5.desc: The rule you never forget: 14 AWG → 15A, 12 AWG → 20A, 10 AWG → 30A. And nothing gets swapped without lockout.
m5.s1: The [[breaker]] protects the WIRE. Rule: **14 AWG → 15A**, **12 AWG → 20A**, **10 AWG → 30A**. If the breaker is bigger than the wire can handle, the wire overheats before the breaker [[trip]]s. That's how fires start.
m5.s2: Connect each cable to its correct breaker. Drag from the cable to the breaker.
m5.w1420: No! 14 AWG on 20A: the wire overheats. 14 goes with 15A.
m5.w1430: Danger! 14 AWG on 30A is a fire waiting to happen. 14 goes with 15A.
m5.w1230: No! 12 AWG on 30A overheats. 12 goes with 20A.
m5.w1215: Not dangerous, but you waste the wire and it trips needlessly. 12 goes with 20A.
m5.w1015: 10 AWG is for 30A. On 15A it trips all the time.
m5.s3: The homeowner put a 30A breaker on a 12 AWG circuit “because it kept tripping”. What do you do?
m5.s3a: Leave it; it doesn't trip anymore.
m5.s3aFb: It doesn't trip because now the wire overheats unprotected. Fire risk.
m5.s3b: Put a 20A back and find out why the circuit is overloaded.
m5.s3bFb: Correct. It tripped from [[overload]]: the problem is the load, not the breaker.
m5.s3c: Put in a 40A so it never trips.
m5.s3cFb: Even worse. You size the breaker for the wire, never for the load.
m5.s4: Swap that breaker for a 20. — What do you do FIRST?
m5.s4a: Swap it with the panel energized, very carefully.
m5.failHot: You worked in an energized panel. One slip of the screwdriver on the [[bus]] and it's an arc flash: severe burns or death. First: [[kill_the_main]], [[lockout_tagout]] with YOUR lock, and [[verify_dead]] with your tester.
m5.s4b: Turn off just that breaker and swap it.
m5.failBus: Turning off one breaker doesn't de-energize the panel: the [[bus]] it clips onto is still live. You touched an energized bus. First: [[kill_the_main]], [[lockout_tagout]] and [[verify_dead]].
m5.s4c: Kill the main, put my lock and tag on it ([[lockout_tagout]]), and verify dead with my tester.
m5.s4cFb: That's how it's done. In Module 2 you'll do it on a real panel.
m5.s5: You're running a 20A circuit for the kitchen receptacles. Which cable?
m5.s5aFb: 14 AWG is only good for 15A. On 20A it overheats.
m5.s5cFb: That's low-voltage control wire. Never for receptacles.
m5.s6: You finished Module 1! You know your tools, gauges, colors and the 14→15, 12→20, 10→30 rule. Next: the 200A panel, where lockout/tagout is for real.
